## Background

All functions in R at least 3 things:

- a *name* (we pick that and use it to call a function)
- input *arguments* (one or more comma seperated inputs that go inside the brackets and we call the function)
- the *body* (the lines of R code that do the work of the function)

# A first function

Here we will create a function 'add() to add numbers together.

> **Q1a.**Your first version of the function should add two input numbers together. For example, add(4, 7) should return 11. $$1 pt$$

```{r}
add <- function(x,y=0) {
 x + y  
  
}
```

Let's test our new function

```{r}
add(x=4,y=7)
```

How about:

```{r}
add(10)
```

```{r}
#Add two input numbers together
add <- function(x,y=0,z=0) {
 x + y + z
  
}
```

```{r}
add(10,10,100)
```

> **Q1b** For you second version, adapt your first function so it can take a single input vector or two inputs as before. For example, add(4, 7) and add( c(4,7,10) ). $$1 pt$$

```{r}
#Add two numbers or add all values in a vector
add <- function(x,y=0) {
 sum(x + y)
  } 
  
```

```{r}
add( c(4,7,10) )
```

```{r}
add(4, 7)
```

> **Q1c** Finally, on your own (outside of class) create a third version of your function that can add any number of inputs that the user provides. For example, add(1, 2, 3, -4) should return 2. Hint: explore the ... (dots) argument or the base R function sum(). $$2 pts$$

```{r}
#Add any number of input values

add<- function(...) {
  sum(...)
}
  add(4,7)
  add(c(4,7,10))
  add(1,2,3,-4)

```

## A generate DNA function

Write a function generate_dna() that returns a random DNA sequence of a length specified by the user.

> **Q2a** Your first version should return a multi-element vector of single character nucleotides. For example generate_dna(6) might return "A", "T", "T", "G", "A", "C". $$1 pt$$

Useful base R functions that you may (or may not) find useful for this lab include: sample(), paste(), paste0(), if(), for(), sapply(), nchar(), and cat().

The 'sample()' function looks useful. There are two **required arguments** (i.e. inputs I must give that dint have a default value)

```{r}
sample(x=1:10, size=4)
```

We can use this with "A" "C" "G" and "T" as input x to make random nucleotide sequences:

```{r}
sample(x=c("A","C","G","T"),size=15, replace=TRUE)
```

We have a working sniped of code that does something useful! This can serve as the "body" of our first 'generate_dna()' function.

```{r}
#Make a random DNA sequence
generate_dna <- function(len){sample(x=c("A","C","G","T"),size=len, replace=TRUE)}
  
```

```{r}
generate_dna(6)
```

> Q2b Your second version should optionally be able to return either a multi-element vector of single character nucleotides (as before) or a single character string (not a vector of single letters but a singe vector of multiple letters). For example "AAGGCTG". $$1 pt$$

Useful base R functions that you may (or may not) find useful for this lab include: sample(), paste(), paste0(), if(), for(), sapply(), nchar(), and cat().

```{r}
paste(c("A", "C", "A"),collapse= "")
```

```{r}
flag<-TRUE
if(flag) {cat("Look at me! We are here")}


```

```{r}
generate_dna <- function(len, collapse=FALSE){
  #Make a random DNA sequence with seperate letters.
  s <- sample(x=c("A", "C", "G","T"),size=len, replace=TRUE)
  
  if(collapse) {
  
  #Make a single element vector
  s<-paste(s, collapse="")
    
    #Cat("you picked true")
  }
  return(s)
  }
```

```{r}
generate_dna(6, collapse= F)
generate_dna(6, collapse= T)
generate_dna(6)

```

> **Q2c:** Finally, create a final version of your function that prints out a FASTA format sequence with an id line indicating the sequence length. For example: len9 CGAAGGCTG Be sure to include clear comments that explain each step of your function. $$2 pts$$

```{r}
len<-90
paste(">length",len, sep="")
```

```{r}
generate_dna <- function(len, fasta=FALSE){
  #Multi-element nucleotide vector
  s <- sample(x=c("A", "C", "G","T"),size=len, replace=TRUE)
  
  if(fasta) {
    id<-paste(">len",len, sep="")
  
  #Make a single element vector
  s<-paste(s, collapse="")
    cat(id,s, sep="\n")
  }
  return(s)
  }
```

```{r}
x<- generate_dna(9, fasta=TRUE)
```

> **Q3** Write a function generate_protein() that returns a random peptide/protein sequence of a length specified by the user. For example generate_protein(6) might return "WQRTAG".

```{r}
## From page 1 of lab-sheet
aa<-c("A","R","N","D","C","E","Q","G","H","I", "L","K","M","F","P","S","T","W","Y","V")
```

```{r}
generate_protein <- function(len, fasta=FALSE){
  #Multi-element amino acids 
  
 aa<-c("A","R","N","D","C","E","Q","G","H","I", "L","K","M","F","P","S","T","W","Y","V")
  #Multi-element amino acids vector
 s<- sample(x=aa, size=len, replace=TRUE)
 
 #put the amino acids toegther
 s<-paste(s, collapse="")
  if(fasta) {
     
    
  
  #Add a FASTA> id line
    id<-paste(">length",len, sep="")
  s<-paste(id,s,"\n", sep="\n")
          
    cat(s)
  }
  return(s)
  }

```

```{r}
generate_protein(6)
```

> **Q4** Adapt and use your generate_protein() function to generate a series of random protein sequences ranging from 6 to 13 amino acids in length (one sequence per length). Take advantage of the base R function for() or sapply() so that you do not have to call generate_protein() eight times by hand.

```{r}
X<-generate_protein(6, fasta=T)
X<-generate_protein(7, fasta=T)
X<-generate_protein(8, fasta=T)
X<-generate_protein(9, fasta=T)
X<-generate_protein(10, fasta=T)
X<-generate_protein(11, fasta=T)
X<-generate_protein(12, fasta=T)
X<-generate_protein(13, fasta=T)

```

we can do this with a 'for()' loop. A 'for()' loop iterates

```{r}
for(i in 1:10){
  cat(i,"\n")
}
```

```{r}
#Make random protein sequences from length 6 to 13
for(len in 6:13){
 x<-generate_protein(len,fasta=1)
}
```

We can do this with a 'for()' loop iterates for each element

```{r}
sapply(6:13,generate_protein, fasta=T)
```

## BLASTp search against nr - are our peptides unique in nature?

> **Q5a** At which sequence length do your randomly generated peptides start to look “unique in nature” (i.e. no 100% coverage + 100% identity hit)? [1 pt]

Take your FASTA-formatted peptides from Q4 and run them as a single BLASTp search against the Non-redundant protein sequences (nr) database at <https://blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/>. For this question do not restrict the organism (leave the Organism field blank so that the full nr database is searched).

| Length | %ide   | %cov | Unique(Y/N) |
|--------|--------|------|-------------|
| 6      | 100%   | 100% | N           |
| 7      | 100%   | 100% | N           |
| 8      | 87.50% | 100% | Y           |
| 9      | 100%   | 78%  | Y           |
| 10     | 100%   | 90%  | Y           |
| 11     | 80%    | 91%  | Y           |
| 12     | 90.91% | 83%  | Y           |
| 13     | 76.92% | 92%  | Y           |

At eight amino acids, my randomly generated peptides start to look unique in nature because this is the first length that does not have both 100% identity and 100% coverage.

> **Q5b** Speculate why very short random peptides are almost always found in nr, while longer ones typically are not. Your answer should refer both to the size of the sequence space (20𝐿 for a peptide of length 𝐿) and to the size of the known protein universe. [1 pt]

Because there are fewer possible sequences, short peptides are more likely to be found in the database.The possibilty of finding a match in the known proteins decrease as peptides longer because the number of possible sequences (20 L) increases significanlty.

> **Q6** In 3–6 sentences total and using your Q5 data and the reasoning from Q5b, what do you think this minimum length is and why might it be a bad design choice for the immune system to present very short peptides? [3 pt]

I think the minimum peptide lenght is about 8 amino acids based on my Q5 results because that is when the peptides begin to look unique. Because there are fewer possible sequences for short peptides, they are more likely to match to proteins already found in nature. Longer peptides are easier to distinguish since they have more possible sequences. The immune system may find it more difficult to distinguish between the bodys own protein and foreign proteins if very short peptides are introduced and it may mistakenly target its own cells.
